title: Setting Up Spring Security
description: Add the Spring Security starter and see the default behavior.

slides.title: Add the Starter 📦
slides.content:
# Dependencies

In your `pom.xml`, add:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

Now restart your application. What happens? All endpoints become **secured by default** with a generated password!

quizData.question: What does Spring Boot automatically do when you add spring‑boot‑starter‑security?

options.text: It opens all endpoints without authentication
It secures all endpoints with a default username and a generated password
It asks you to configure a login page

quizData.explanation: Spring Boot's auto‑configuration secures all endpoints with Basic Auth, providing a default user 'user' and a random password logged at startup.

slides.title: Default Behavior in Action
slides.content:
Run your app and try to access any endpoint, e.g., `http://localhost:8080/hello`. You'll see a login prompt (or a 401 if using REST clients).

Check the logs for the generated password:
```
Using generated security password: 12345abc...
```

Username is `user`. Try it!

This is Spring Security's default auto‑configuration, but we'll replace it with custom settings.

slides.title: Disable Auto‑Config Temporarily
slides.content: If you want to see only your own configuration, add `@EnableWebSecurity` and provide a `SecurityFilterChain` bean. We'll do that next.
